name: Ilkhanate
summary: The Mongol khanate of Iran founded by Hulegu, who sacked Baghdad in 1258. Its rulers converted to Islam in 1295 and sponsored Persian art and science.

location.value: Iran, Iraq, the South Caucasus and much of Anatolia.

terrain.value: The Iranian plateau, the Mesopotamian plain and the highlands of the Caucasus and Anatolia.
terrain.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

climate.value: Mostly arid; Mongol herds needed the pastures of Azerbaijan.
climate.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

resources.value: Farmland, pasture and control of trade between Europe and China.
resources.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

disasters.value: The Black Death ravaged the Ilkhanate in the 1330s.

population.value: No reliable estimate; Mongol campaigns had caused heavy losses before it was founded.
population.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

urbanisation.value: Capitals at Maragheh, Tabriz and Soltaniyeh.

migration.value: Mongol and Turkic nomads settled in north-western Iran.
migration.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

economicBase.value: Farming and taxes, which were reformed under Ghazan.
economicBase.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

tradeRoutes.value: Tabriz was a great hub between Europe, India and China.
tradeRoutes.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

moneyAndTax.value: Silver coins; an attempt at Chinese-style paper money (1294) failed.
moneyAndTax.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

inequality.value: A Mongol elite and Persian officials ruled over peasants.
inequality.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

governmentType.value: Monarchy under a khan (later padishah), at first under the Great Khan.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

keyRulers.value: Hulegu (1256–1265), Abaqa, Ghazan (1295–1304), Öljaitü, Abu Sa‘id (1316–1335).

succession.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

institutions.value: Ghazan’s reforms of tax and administration, led by vizier Rashid al-Din.
institutions.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

stability.value: Disintegrated after Abu Sa‘id’s death in 1335.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

eliteConflict.value: Mongol emirs fought for control of the court.
eliteConflict.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

armyAndTech.value: Mongol cavalry with Chinese and Persian siege engineers.
armyAndTech.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

majorWars.value: Sack of Baghdad (1258), defeat at Ain Jalut (1260), war with the Golden Horde (1262).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Mamluks and the Golden Horde; diplomatic contacts with European powers.
alliancesRivals.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

scienceEducation.value: Rashid al-Din’s “Compendium of Chronicles”, a world history.
scienceEducation.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

openness.value: Brought Chinese astronomers and doctors to the court.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

religion.value: Buddhism and shamanism among the rulers until Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

artsArchitecture.value: The dome of Soltaniyeh and Persian miniature painting with Chinese influences.
artsArchitecture.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

socialStructure.value: Mongol nobles, Persian bureaucrats, merchants and peasants.
socialStructure.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

neighbours.value: The Mamluks, Golden Horde, Byzantium and the Chagatai Khanate.
neighbours.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

ideasReligions.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

colonisation.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

riseSignals.value: Hulegu’s conquest of Iran and Baghdad.

peakPeriod.source: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

declineSignals.value: No heir after Abu Sa‘id, and the Black Death.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Ilkhanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

outcome.value: Disintegrated into regional dynasties (Jalayirids, Chobanids and others); later the Timurids.

knownFor.label: Maragheh observatory
knownFor.note: A great observatory led by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi.

knownFor.label: Dome of Soltaniyeh
knownFor.note: One of the largest brick domes in the world.
